results.result: The authors demonstrate that cohesion establishment in S. cerevisiae occurs via two distinct mechanisms: (1) conversion of cohesin associated with un-replicated DNA, requiring Tof1/Csm3, Ctf4, and Chl1 but not Scc2, and (2) Scc2-dependent de novo loading at replication forks, requiring the Ctf18-RFC complex. Each pathway requires a different set of replisome-associated proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C8 and C70-C74 collectively establish the existence of two distinct cohesion establishment pathways with different protein requirements. The experimental data using non-cleavable cohesin, temperature-sensitive mutants, and mini-chromosome assays (Figures 2-5) provide converging evidence for this central finding. The Scc2-independence of conversion (C72, C84) and Ctf18-RFC requirement for de novo loading (C73, C119) are demonstrated through multiple complementary experiments.

results.result: Cohesin associated with un-replicated chromosomes during G2/M is converted into cohesive structures (CDs) during S phase in the absence of Scc2 activity. Both wild-type and scc2-45 cells produce similar amounts of CDs when cohesin loaded during G2/M undergoes replication, demonstrating Scc2-independent conversion.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C84 describe the key experiment demonstrating Scc2-independent conversion (Figure 2B). The observation that both SCC2 and scc2-45 cells produce CDs from G2/M-loaded cohesin provides direct evidence for conversion. The reduction in CMs in scc2-45 cells (C82) supports the conversion model, though the higher CM levels in wild-type cells (C83) suggest some de novo loading also occurs.

results.result: Deletion of mrc1, chl1, ctf4, csm3, tof1, or ctf18 does not affect CD formation when endogenous cohesin is expressed throughout G1 and S phase. However, chl1Δ, ctf4Δ, csm3Δ, and tof1Δ cells completely fail to produce CDs from cohesin loaded during G2/M, while ctf18Δ and mrc1Δ cells form CDs normally, demonstrating that Chl1, Ctf4, and Csm3/Tof1 are specifically required for the conversion pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C93 describe the differential requirements for conversion versus total cohesion establishment (Figure 3). The complete absence of CDs in chl1Δ, ctf4Δ, csm3Δ, and tof1Δ mutants when cohesin is loaded in G2/M (C90) contrasts with normal CD formation in ctf18Δ and mrc1Δ cells (C89), providing strong evidence for pathway-specific protein requirements. The observation that these proteins are also required to prevent cohesin dissociation during S phase (C93) adds mechanistic insight.

results.result: Chl1, Ctf4, and Csm3/Tof1 are essential for maintaining cohesin on chromosomes during S phase. In chl1Δ cells, a small fraction of cohesin persists after S phase due to Scc2-dependent re-loading, while in chl1Δ scc2-45 double mutants, nearly all pre-existing chromosomal cohesin disappears. ChIP-seq data confirm that half or more of cohesin loaded during G2/M disappears genome-wide when chl1Δ cells undergo S phase.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C108 demonstrate that conversion pathway proteins maintain cohesin on chromosomes during replication (Figure 4). The complete loss of cohesin-DNA interactions in chl1Δ scc2-45 double mutants (C102, C107) versus partial retention in chl1Δ single mutants (C102, C106) provides strong evidence that the small amount of persisting cohesin arises from Scc2-dependent re-loading (C104). The genome-wide ChIP-seq data (C105-C107) extend the mini-chromosome findings to the entire genome.

results.result: When non-cleavable cohesin is expressed during S phase (rather than G2/M), chl1Δ, ctf4Δ, csm3Δ, and tof1Δ mutants form CDs normally, demonstrating that the timing of cohesin synthesis determines pathway usage. The de novo pathway requires Scc2, as chl1Δ scc2-45 double mutants fail to form any cohesin-DNA interactions when cohesin is expressed during S phase at the restrictive temperature.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C113 establish that conversion pathway mutants can form cohesion via the de novo pathway when cohesin is synthesized during S phase (Figure 5A-B). The identical CD formation in wild-type and mutant cells when cohesin is expressed during S phase (C109) demonstrates that the defect is specific to conversion. The complete absence of cohesin-DNA interactions in chl1Δ scc2-45 cells (C112) provides direct evidence for Scc2 requirement in the de novo pathway (C113).

results.result: The de novo cohesion establishment pathway requires the Ctf18-RFC complex. In chl1Δ ctf8-17 double mutants at the restrictive temperature, CD formation is abolished while CM formation remains normal, indicating that Scc2 can load cohesin onto individual DNA molecules but cannot entrap sister DNAs within the same ring without Ctf18-RFC. Inactivation of both pathways causes lethality.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C121 demonstrate Ctf18-RFC requirement for the de novo pathway (Figure 5C). The synthetic lethality of combining conversion and de novo pathway mutants (C114, C121) establishes that both pathways are essential. The differential effect on CDs versus CMs in chl1Δ ctf8-17 cells (C115-C116) provides strong evidence that Ctf18-RFC is specifically required for sister DNA co-entrapment during de novo loading (C118-C119), not for cohesin loading per se.

results.result: CHL1 overexpression suppresses cohesion defects in ctf8Δ cells (reducing precocious sister chromatid separation from 47% to 18%) but has minimal effect in ctf4Δ cells (49% to 40%), demonstrating that augmentation of the conversion pathway can compensate for de novo pathway defects. CHL1 overexpression does not compensate for defective conversion caused by ctf4Δ, consistent with Chl1's chromatin association depending on Ctf4.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C129 demonstrate pathway-specific suppression by CHL1 overexpression (Figure 6A). The marked suppression of ctf8Δ cohesion defects (C125) versus minimal effect on ctf4Δ (C126) provides strong evidence that CHL1 overexpression specifically augments the conversion pathway (C127). The lack of suppression in ctf4Δ cells (C128) is consistent with Chl1's dependence on Ctf4 for chromatin association (C129), though this latter claim relies primarily on prior work.

results.result: An additional copy of SCC2 increases the fitness of ctf4Δ cells but not ctf18Δ cells, demonstrating that modest Scc2 overexpression specifically enhances the de novo loading pathway. Conversely, CHL1 overexpression augments the conversion pathway. Augmentation of either pathway suppresses defects caused by abrogation of the other pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C138 demonstrate pathway-specific enhancement by SCC2 overexpression (Figure 6B). The differential fitness effects on ctf4Δ versus ctf18Δ cells (C133-C134) provide strong evidence that Scc2 overexpression specifically enhances the de novo pathway (C135-C136). The reciprocal suppression patterns (CHL1 overexpression suppresses de novo pathway defects, SCC2 overexpression suppresses conversion pathway defects) support the existence of two independent pathways (C138).

results.result: The division of replisome proteins into two epistasis groups (Chl1/Ctf4/Csm3/Tof1 versus Mrc1/Ctf18-RFC) corresponds precisely with their roles in conversion versus de novo loading pathways. Combining mutants from the same group has minimal additional effects, while combining mutants from different groups causes synthetic lethality or sickness, demonstrating that conversion is not the sole mechanism for cohesion establishment and that a second mechanism involving Mrc1 and Ctf18-RFC can generate cohesion in the absence of conversion.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 and C94-C97 connect the current findings to prior epistasis analysis. The correspondence between epistasis groups and pathway requirements (C94) provides strong support for the two-pathway model. The observation that conversion pathway proteins form a single epistasis group because they share a specific function (C95) is well-supported by the data. The inference that conversion is not the sole mechanism (C96) and that a second mechanism exists (C97) is strongly supported by the experimental evidence, though C97 relies partly on prior synthetic lethality data.

results.result: Cohesion establishment is confined to S phase. Cohesin can load onto chromosomes throughout the cell cycle, but it only builds cohesion during S phase. Cohesin loaded in post-replicative G2 cells can entrap individual DNAs but cannot form cohesion or entrap sister DNAs.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C50-C51, and C78 establish the S-phase specificity of cohesion establishment. These claims are well-supported by prior work (C50, C78 cite previous studies) and are consistent with the experimental design of the current study. The observation that G2-loaded cohesin forms CMs but not CDs (C78) is central to the conversion assay design and is repeatedly demonstrated in the experimental data.

results.result: Cohesin loaded during G2/M does not require Scc2 to prevent its release from chromosomes, and this property is maintained when cells enter the subsequent G1 phase (as long as kleisin is non-cleavable). The median level of G2/M-loaded cohesin remains constant during extended G1 arrest, implying that G1 cells inherit little or no free nucleoplasmic cohesin that could load during this period.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C77 and C79-C80 describe the unusual Scc2-independence of G2/M-loaded cohesin, which is crucial for the experimental design. These claims are supported by prior work (citations to Srinivasan et al., 2019) and are validated by the current experiments. Claims C144-C145 provide additional support through ChIP-seq data showing constant cohesin levels during G1 arrest (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), confirming that no new loading occurs during this period.

results.result: Catenation by cohesin of individual DNAs creates catenated monomers (CMs) with modestly retarded electrophoretic migration, while co-entrapment of sister DNAs creates catenated dimers (CDs) with greatly retarded migration. CD formation accompanies cohesion establishment in all cases analyzed, suggesting that co-entrapment within cohesin's Smc-kleisin ring may be the mechanism by which cohesin holds sister DNAs together.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C26 and C31-C32 describe the CM/CD assay that is central to the study. The electrophoretic behavior of CMs and CDs (C25-C26) is well-established by prior work (citations provided). The correlation between CD formation and cohesion establishment (C31) is stated as an observation from prior analyses and is consistent with the current findings. The inference that co-entrapment is the cohesion mechanism (C32) is presented as a hypothesis and is appropriately qualified.

results.result: All six replisome protein deletions (mrc1Δ, chl1Δ, ctf4Δ, csm3Δ, tof1Δ, ctf18Δ) cause modest cohesion defects when measured by GFP-based cytological assays, but cells lacking individual replisome proteins can generate and maintain mini-chromosome cohesion when cohesin is expressed from its endogenous promoter. The 6C mini-chromosome assay is less sensitive to minor cohesion defects than GFP-based assays, possibly because mini-chromosomes are small (2.3 kb) and contain centromeres that act as potent cohesin loading sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 and C146-C147 address the apparent discrepancy between mini-chromosome and chromosomal locus assays. The observation that all deletions cause modest defects by GFP assay (C87, citing prior work) but not by mini-chromosome assay (C147, current data) is clearly documented. The inference that mini-chromosomes are less sensitive (C88) is reasonable, and the proposed explanation involving mini-chromosome size and centromere content (C146) is plausible though not directly tested.

results.result: Maintenance of sister chromatid cohesion depends on abrogation of Wapl-induced release through Smc3 acetylation by Eco1. In yeast, Smc3 acetylation occurs only during S phase and is sufficient to block release, while in mammalian cells, both Smc3 acetylation and sororin association are necessary. Eco1 is required to build cohesion during S phase but not to maintain it during G2, and Eco1 acetyl transferases are largely dispensable in cells lacking Wapl across yeast, mammalian, and plant species.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C49 describe the role of Eco1/Smc3 acetylation in cohesion maintenance. These claims are well-supported by extensive prior work (multiple citations provided for each claim). The species-specific differences in acetylation sufficiency (C42-C45) and the dispensability of Eco1 in Wapl-deficient cells (C47-C49) are established findings that provide important context for the current study. These claims are appropriately presented as background knowledge.

results.result: Multiple replisome-associated proteins (Ctf4, Chl1, Csm3/Tof1, Mrc1, Ctf18-RFC) have important but non-essential roles in cohesion establishment. These proteins are not necessary for DNA replication but are all associated with the replisome and are highly conserved among eukaryotes. Inactivation during G2/M has no effect on cohesion maintenance, and expression of Chl1 during G2/M cannot rescue cohesion defects caused by its absence during replication.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C60 and C64-C69 provide essential background on replisome proteins involved in cohesion. These claims are well-supported by extensive prior work (multiple citations for each protein). The non-essentiality for replication (C64), replisome association (C65), S-phase specificity (C66-C67), and evolutionary conservation (C68-C69) are established findings that motivate the current study. These claims appropriately set up the central question of how these proteins contribute to cohesion establishment.
